title: AI Tools Have the Potential to Widen the Performance Gap Between High and Low Performers
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article challenges the assumption that generative AI automatically levels the playing field between strong and weak performers. Citing research on business owners, it shows that AI boosted outcomes substantially for already-successful users but caused declines for struggling ones, because low performers tend to follow generic AI advice uncritically while high performers use it more skeptically as one input among many. The piece frames this as a judgment problem, not a tool problem, since AI amplifies whatever quality of thinking a person brings to it. It closes with a call for leaders to actively coach people on when to trust AI output and when to question it.
points: AI tools help most with well-defined tasks, but their value in open-ended, judgment-heavy work depends on who is using them.
One study found AI raised profits 15% for already-successful business owners but caused a nearly 10% decline for struggling ones.
Low performers tend to act on generic AI advice without critically evaluating it, weakening their outcomes.
High performers stay skeptical of AI recommendations, using the tool to sharpen judgment rather than replace it.
Leaders risk widening performance gaps unless they train people on when to trust AI and when to question it.
quotes: When team members use AI to augment their work, both high and low performers benefit from the ideas, strategies, and suggestions the tools produce.
In contexts where problems are broad, complex, or fuzzy, AI doesn't replace human judgment — it amplifies it.
In one study, AI boosted revenues and profits by 15 percent among business owners who were already successful.
These low performers act on the AI guidance without thinking critically about it. To their detriment.
AI deployments actually risk widening performance gaps, because the people who need it the most are usually the least equipped to filter and apply the advice it offers.
